summaries.example: Imagine that a notebook says, “One thinker says the sun is this size; another says it is that size.” The notebook may not decide who is right. It simply saves the different ideas so someone can study and compare them. Ancient doxographies often worked in a similar way.
summaries.summary: Doxography is the study and reporting of ancient philosophers’ ideas. Most Greek and Roman philosophy writings have been lost, but later writers preserved pieces of information about them. Some collections arrange short views by subject, such as the motion of the earth or the causes of illness. Other works give more space to whole schools, their founders, and their arguments. A famous nineteenth-century scholar, Hermann Diels, tried to trace many reports back through earlier writers to Theophrastus, a student of Aristotle. Later study showed that parts of this picture are useful but that some links are uncertain. Aristotle’s way of sorting and comparing earlier opinions may have helped shape these collections. Doxographies are valuable, but they are not perfect copies of the original ideas. Writers could shorten, rearrange, update, or change material. We should therefore use them as evidence while also asking how the evidence was transmitted and what the writer was trying to do.
key_ideas: Many ancient philosophy books disappeared, so later reports help us learn about lost ideas.
Doxographies collect philosophers’ views, often by topic, such as the stars, health, or the mind.
Some reports list opposing ideas without choosing a winner.
Scholars compare surviving writings to reconstruct older works and judge how dependable each report is.
summaries.why_it_matters: Doxography helps us learn about thinkers whose own books no longer survive. It also teaches an important research lesson: an old report is not automatically a complete or exact record. To understand the past, we need to compare sources, notice their organization, and consider how they may have changed.

important_terms.definition: A report or collection that records what philosophers or schools believed about questions.
A person’s idea or belief about a question.
A short version made from a longer work.
Careful study of where a report came from and how it changed as people copied it.

questions_to_think_about: If a notebook records two different answers, does that mean both answers are true?
Why might a copied report change over time?
What clues could help you decide whether an old report is trustworthy?

summaries.example: Suppose a surviving summary says that earlier thinkers disagreed about whether the cosmos had one system or several. The summary presents the alternatives but does not settle the question. A historian should not treat the list as a transparent transcript of each original view. The arrangement may reflect the compiler’s method, and later copying or updating may have altered the wording and selection of doctrines.
summaries.summary: Ancient doxography concerns reports of philosophical positions. In its broad use, the term can cover discussions in Cicero, Diogenes Laërtius, and other writers who describe schools, doctrines, biographies, or arguments. In its narrower use, emphasized in Hermann Diels’ Doxographi Graeci, it refers especially to concise, theme-based lists of contrasting positions in natural philosophy. Diels argued that later witnesses, including the work preserved as ps-Plutarch’s Placita and excerpts in Stobaeus, ultimately depended on earlier collections, notably a work attributed to Aëtius and, further back, Theophrastus’ supposed Physikôn Doxai. This reconstruction remains influential, but the entry stresses that several stages are uncertain. Similar wording does not by itself prove direct descent, and some later reports appear to reshape doctrines attributed to philosophers whose works survive. Aristotle provides a significant alternative background: he regularly surveys earlier opinions, classifies them by systematic divisions, tests agreements and conflicts, and then proceeds toward a solution. Theophrastus developed related practices. Thus the form of the Placita may reflect a broader Peripatetic method rather than a simple chain of faithful copying. Doxographies usually offer a status of the question rather than a verdict. They are tools for inquiry, but their evidence must be assessed in light of transmission, editorial purpose, organization, and adaptation.
key_ideas: In the broad sense, doxography includes many reports of philosophical views; in the narrow sense associated with Diels, it mainly concerns brief, subject-arranged reports in natural philosophy.
Diels reconstructed a chain running from Theophrastus through proposed intermediate collections to later witnesses such as ps-Plutarch and Stobaeus.
The entry questions parts of Diels’ reconstruction, especially the confident link from later reports back to a single Theophrastean foundation.
Aristotle’s practice of classifying and evaluating earlier opinions offers an important background for understanding the structure of later collections.
Doxographies can preserve valuable information while also adapting, distorting, or modernizing the views they report.
Their usefulness depends on studying transmission, arrangement, purpose, and the relationship among surviving witnesses.
summaries.why_it_matters: The study of doxography shows how historical knowledge is built from incomplete and mediated evidence. It prevents two opposite mistakes: dismissing later summaries as useless, or treating every surviving line as an untouched fragment of a lost original. Careful source criticism can recover patterns in ancient philosophy while preserving appropriate uncertainty about attribution, dependence, and accuracy.

important_terms.definition: A secondary report that presents philosophers’ views or doctrines, rather than primarily developing the reporter’s own philosophical position.
A view, thesis, or doctrine attributed to a philosopher or school.
A method of dividing a field into sets, subsets, and further distinctions in order to classify and compare positions.
A structured overview that sets competing positions beside one another, often as preparation for inquiry or criticism.
A proposed chain of dependence connecting a later report to earlier sources or documents.
A short work or passage produced by condensing a longer source.
A state of disagreement in which competing positions appear to block a decisive conclusion.
A text or collection used as evidence about earlier works, while still requiring interpretation and evaluation.

questions_to_think_about: Why does arranging views by topic produce different evidence from arranging them by philosopher or school?
When does resemblance between two reports justify inferring a shared source?
How might a compiler’s categories affect the content of the views being reported?
Can a collection that gives no final answer still be useful to someone seeking one?
What would make a reconstructed ancient document more or less convincing?

summaries.example: Think of a class website that collects students’ answers to “What causes a storm?” One page sorts answers by idea, while another sorts them by student. A third page shortens the answers and adds newer ones. These pages could help a teacher understand the discussion, but they would not be perfect copies of what each student originally said. Ancient doxographies raised a similar problem for historians.
summaries.summary: Doxography means reporting philosophical views. The word is used broadly today for many ancient works that describe ideas about nature, ethics, knowledge, schools, or other subjects. In a narrower sense, it describes brief collections that place different views next to one another by topic. This matters because much ancient Greek and Roman philosophy has disappeared. Later reports sometimes preserve clues about those lost works. Hermann Diels made an influential attempt to reconstruct how these reports were connected. He argued that collections such as ps-Plutarch’s Placita and parts of Stobaeus came through earlier stages, including a work by Aëtius and, ultimately, a book by Theophrastus. The entry does not simply accept every part of this explanation. Some proposed links are uncertain, and a resemblance between passages does not automatically prove that they came from the same original book. Aristotle offers important background. He often began by listing earlier opinions, sorting them into groups, comparing disagreements, and then investigating the problem himself. Theophrastus used related methods. Later collections may therefore reflect organized philosophical debate, not just mechanical copying. Doxographies are useful tools, but they can be shortened, rearranged, updated, or distorted. Readers must ask who assembled a report, how it was passed down, and what purpose it served.
key_ideas: Ancient writers often reported what philosophers believed, and these reports are important because many original works are lost.
Doxography can be broad, including discussions of schools and ethics, or narrow, meaning short topic-by-topic reports in natural philosophy.
Hermann Diels proposed that many later reports descended through a chain of earlier sources reaching back to Theophrastus.
The entry explains that Diels’ theory is partly helpful but too confident in some places, because similar passages may have more than one possible origin.
Aristotle and Theophrastus organized earlier opinions by divisions and contrasts, which may explain the shape of later collections.
A doxography may show the competing answers to a question without deciding which answer is correct.
summaries.why_it_matters: Doxography helps us study ideas that survive only indirectly. It also shows why historical reading requires judgment. A report can preserve a genuine clue while still changing the original view. Comparing several witnesses and examining their structure gives us a better chance of understanding ancient philosophy without pretending that all the evidence is equally certain.

important_terms.definition: A work or section that reports the views of philosophers or philosophical schools.
A belief, claim, or doctrine held by a thinker or school.
A shortened version of a longer text.
A way of dividing and organizing ideas into groups and smaller groups.
The study of how a text was copied, shortened, combined, or changed as it passed through history.
A proposed earlier text used to explain similarities among later reports.

questions_to_think_about: How is a list of opinions different from an argument for one opinion?
Why might a writer arrange ideas by subject instead of by philosopher?
What can similarities between two old texts tell us—and what can they not prove?
Why should historians be cautious when using a short summary of a lost book?
